chunks.title: Tokenised stocks, priced two ways
chunks.text: The Gully Labs tracker checks every tokenised stock on Robinhood Chain and BNB Chain against its fair price, live. These docs cover how it works, the public API it is built on, and the widget that puts it on your own page. Docs for the Gully Labs stock token tracker: how its fair and onchain prices are read, the public API, the embeddable widget and API keys.

chunks.title: Tokenised stocks, priced two ways
chunks.text: For each stock token the tracker reads two prices: the fair price, from the Chainlink feed for that stock, read on chain; and the onchain price, what the token trades at in its deepest pool. The difference, as a percentage of fair, is the gap. A token trading above its fair price is at a premium; below it, at a discount. The live page is at gullylabs.xyz/tracker. Everything it shows comes from the same public API these docs describe.

chunks.title: Tokenised stocks, priced two ways
chunks.text: Fair prices are Chainlink feeds read on chain with latestRoundData(). Onchain prices are read from each token’s deepest pool on chain; DexScreener and GeckoTerminal only find the pool. Nothing is estimated or typed in: a price that cannot be read is reported as unreadable, never as zero. The methodology gives the exact rules. The tracker reports what two public sources say. It is not investment advice, and a gap is not a promise that anyone can trade it away.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: How each number is read, how the gap is computed, and the rules that keep a small pool or a closed market from making a headline. How the Gully Labs tracker reads a stock token's fair price from Chainlink and its onchain price from the deepest pool, and the rules that decide when a gap is flagged.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: For every token in the tracker’s feed table, on every chain it covers, two numbers are read live on each refresh: Fair: the Chainlink feed for that stock, read on chain. Onchain: the token’s price in its deepest pool, read straight from that pool’s contract. Both are in US dollars per token. Each is either a number or unreadable; an unreadable price is never replaced with zero or with an older figure.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: Every feed is read with latestRoundData() in one batched call per chain. A round whose answer is zero or negative, or whose update time is zero, counts as unreadable. The answer is scaled by the feed’s decimals. Robinhood Chain The feeds price the token itself (feedPrices: "tokenized-instrument"), so fair is the feed’s answer. BNB Chain The feeds price the underlying share (feedPrices: "underlying-share"). One raw bStock token is a number of shares given by the token’s own uiMultiplier() (ERC-8056, where 1e18 means 1.0). The multiplier is read on chain on every refresh, because the issuer changes it at a split. If the multiplier cannot be read, or reads as zero, the fair price is unreadable for that token. The multiplier used is returned in each row as multiplier.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: Once an hour the tracker asks DexScreener (GeckoTerminal if DexScreener refuses) for every pool of every token, 30 tokens per request. For each token it keeps the pools with a positive price and picks one: pools quoted against a native coin or a dollar stablecoin come first (WETH, ETH, WBNB, BNB, USDC, USDG, USDT, USD1, FDUSD), then the deepest by liquidity. Between those reads, every refresh prices the chosen pool from the chain itself: slot0() on a v3 pool, StateView.getSlot0 on a Uniswap v4 pool. The pool’s ratio is turned into dollars with $1 for a dollar stablecoin, Chainlink’s ETH/USD or BNB/USD feed for the native coin, and this cycle’s fair price where the quote is itself a stock token. The chain’s poolSource says on chain when this is the source. The row’s pool object names the pool used, its liquidity and 24-hour volume, and totals across every pool found for the token. Liquidity and volume come from the hourly read, because the chain does not publish them in a usable form.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: Every row carries a status, decided in this order: feed-unreadable (fair is null): The Chainlink feed (or, on BNB Chain, the multiplier) could not be read. pool-unreadable (pool read failed): DexScreener could not be read for this chain. no-pool (onchain is null): No pool with a usable price was found. unverified (onchain ≥ 5× or ≤ 1/5 of fair; or |gap| ≥ 15% unless the pool holds $1,000,000+ and was read on chain this cycle): The figure is implausible for a tokenised stock: far more often a bad print (a misread venue, an old API reading, a decimals slip) than a price. gapPct is withheld (null), the figure stays in rawGapPct, and untrustedReason says why. Never flagged, ranked, alerted on or recorded in the history. thin (liquidity < $10,000): The chosen pool is too small to trust. Shown, never flagged. in-line (|gap| < 1%): Within the noise. Robinhood Chain feeds only move on a 0.5% deviation. drifting (1% ≤ |gap| < 2%): Moving away from fair, not yet flagged. premium (gap ≥ 2%): Flagged: trading above fair. discount (gap ≤ −2%): Flagged: trading below fair. The thresholds are returned with every response in rules (minLiquidityUsd, inLinePct, flagPct, implausiblePct, trustLiquidityUsd, unitsRatio), so a client never has to hard-code them. Trust and provenance

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: Flagged: trading below fair. The thresholds are returned with every response in rules (minLiquidityUsd, inLinePct, flagPct, implausiblePct, trustLiquidityUsd, unitsRatio), so a client never has to hard-code them. Trust and provenance Every row says whether the tracker stands behind its gap. trusted is true only for premium, discount, drifting and in-line rows whose pool read is fresh; otherwise untrustedReason gives the reason in a sentence (a thin pool, an implausible figure, an unreadable source, or a pool read served from the last good one while sources back off). Top movers and gap alerts only ever use trusted rows; the five-minute history skips every row without a gap (an unverified row included) and every stale pool read. onchainSource says where this cycle’s onchain price came from: chain when the pool contract was read directly, api when it is the price API’s reading for a venue that cannot be re-read on chain. onchainAt is when that price was read, so an API reading shows its own age.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: Stock feeds follow market hours. Each chain reports whether its session is open now: Robinhood Chain, 24/5: Chainlink’s US equities 24/5 session, Sunday 20:00 to Friday 20:00, New York time. BNB Chain, NYSE hours: 09:30 to 16:00 New York time, Monday to Friday. Outside its session a feed holds its last value, so the gap is measured against the last session’s close, not presented as a live mispricing. Market holidays are not modelled: on a holiday the session reads as open and the feed’s update time, returned as feedUpdatedAt, shows how old the fair price is.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: The tracker reads its sources at most once every two minutes. Every visitor and every API caller share that one read. If the chain cannot be read and neither API answers, that chain backs off (one minute, doubling, at most 30 minutes) and keeps serving its last good pool read, marked poolsStale: true with its time in poolsAsOf, and poolStale: true on each row. A pool read older than six hours is dropped rather than shown. Fair prices stay live throughout. Every five minutes one snapshot per token is recorded, and kept for seven days. Rows without a gap, or with a stale pool read, are not recorded. The history endpoint serves them.

chunks.title: Tracker methodology
chunks.text: The onchain price is one pool’s price as DexScreener reports it, not a volume-weighted average across venues. Liquidity figures are DexScreener’s, in US dollars. Only tokens in the tracker’s verified feed tables are covered; a stock token without a Chainlink feed on its chain does not appear. A gap may not be tradable: pool depth, fees, slippage and issuer rules all stand between a gap and a profit. The tracker reports what Chainlink and the pools say, with the rules above. It is not investment advice and makes no promise about any token.

chunks.text: The whole tracker: every chain, the rules, the sources and one row per token. Top level generatedAt (string (ISO)): When this answer was built. chains (Chain[]): One entry per chain, below. rules (object): The thresholds in force: minLiquidityUsd (pools below are “thin”), inLinePct (gaps below are “in line”), flagPct (gaps at or above are flagged), implausiblePct (a gap this wide needs a deep pool read on chain to be believed), trustLiquidityUsd (how deep that pool must be) and unitsRatio (an onchain price this many times fair, or this fraction of it, is a units error). sources (object): fair and onchain describe the two price sources; tables names the feed table used per chain. rows (Row[]): One per token. See Rows. chains[] key (string): Chain key used everywhere else: robinhood or bsc. id (number): EVM chain id (4663, 56). name (string): Display name. sessionOpen (boolean): Whether the chain’s feed session is open now. See sessions. sessionName (string): 24/5 or NYSE hours. fairMethod (string): How fair is derived on this chain, in words. poolsAsOf (string | null): Time of the pool read in use. poolsStale (boolean): True when the pool read is the last good one, served while every price source for that chain is backing off. poolSource (string | null): Where pool prices came from this cycle: on chain, DexScreener or GeckoTerminal.

chunks.text: chain (string): Chain key. ticker (string): Stock ticker, e.g. NVDA. name (string): Company name. token (string): Token contract address. feed (string): Chainlink feed address. fair (number | null): Fair price in USD per token. feedPrices (string): tokenized-instrument (the feed prices the token) or underlying-share (it prices the share). multiplier (number | null): Shares per token from uiMultiplier() on BNB Chain; 1 on Robinhood Chain; null when the feed could not be read. feedUpdatedAt (string | null): When the feed last updated. feedError (string | null): Why the feed could not be read, if it could not. onchain (number | null): Price in the chosen pool, USD per token. gapPct (number | null): (onchain − fair) / fair × 100. Null unless both prices were read, and null on an unverified row (the figure is withheld; see rawGapPct). rawGapPct (number | null): The same gap before the plausibility check. Equal to gapPct on every row except an unverified one, where it keeps the figure that was withheld. Never chart, rank or alert on it. status (string): One of premium, discount, drifting, in-line, thin, unverified, no-pool, pool-unreadable, feed-unreadable. Rules in the methodology. trusted (boolean): Whether the tracker stands behind this row’s gap: true only for premium, discount, drifting and in-line rows whose pool read is fresh (not poolStale). Top movers and gap alerts use trusted rows only.

chunks.title: API reference
chunks.text: One token’s gap history: a snapshot every five minutes. Seven days are open to everyone; paid plans keep more (see Plans & alerts). chain (string): Chain key, default robinhood. 2 to 12 lowercase letters. ticker (string, required): 1 to 8 letters or dots; case does not matter. days (integer, optional): Window in days, from 1 up to what your plan includes. Without it you get the last seven days, as before. Over your plan’s limit answers 403; past seven days the answer adds days and is not cached publicly. The answer is { chain, ticker, points }, where each point is a tuple [unixSeconds, gapPct, onchain, fair], oldest first. A chain or ticker the tracker does not know returns an empty points array, not an error.

chunks.title: API reference
chunks.text: Top movers: how each token’s gap to fair, and its onchain price, changed over the last hour or day, computed from the same five-minute snapshots as the history. For every token the latest snapshot is compared with the snapshot closest to one window earlier. Only tokens whose status is trusted right now (premium, discount, drifting or in-line) and that have both points are ranked; nothing is interpolated. window (string, optional): 24h (default) or 1h. limit (integer, optional): How many rows per ranking, 1 to 50, default 10. chain (string, optional): Rank one chain only, e.g. bsc. ticker (string, optional): With chain: also return that token’s own change in stock (null when it has none). Top level window (string): 1h or 24h. windowSeconds (number): 3600 or 86400. toleranceSeconds (number): How far the earlier snapshot may sit from exactly one window ago: 15 minutes for 1h, 2 hours for 24h. Further than that and the token is left out. asOf (string | null): The newest snapshot compared. Null when nothing could be compared. from, to (string | null): The comparison times: to is asOf, from one window earlier. Each row carries its own exact pair. eligible (number): Tokens with both points and a trusted status. left (object): Why the others are out: untrusted, noHistory, staleHistory (latest snapshot over 30 minutes old), tooShort. historyHours (number): How many hours the longest series covers.

chunks.text: The Holder Map: who holds a DeepCore launch or a tracked stock token, which of the biggest wallets sent tokens to each other (clusters), what known addresses they are (pools, locks, burn, exchanges, DeepCore and Gully contracts), and a plain-English summary.:chain is robinhood, bsc, base, hyperevm or solana;:token is the token address, or a stock’s ticker. Other tokens answer 404. Counted by the same rate limits and keys as the tracker; answers are cached for five minutes. /api/holders/:chain/:token (JSON): state (ok, or unavailable with a reason when a chain’s holder data is not available yet), nodes (rank, address, share, label, cluster, flags), links, clusters, summary (top10Pct, largestCluster, line, plain), forensics for launches (bundled buyers, deployer share and funding, liquidity lock, riskLine), fair for stocks (value at the real share price, premium), timeline (replay frames), sources and asOf. /api/holders/:chain/:token.csv (CSV): The holder list as CSV (when your plan includes it). /api/holders/:chain/:token/card.png (PNG): A 1200 × 630 share card of the map. chunks.title: API reference
chunks.text: /api/tracker (public, max-age=30, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300): The data itself refreshes about every two minutes. /api/tracker/history (public, max-age=60, s-maxage=120, stale-while-revalidate=600): A new point is added every five minutes. /api/tracker/movers (public, max-age=30, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300): Computed at most once a minute per window. Counted by the same rate limit. Answers are cacheable at the edge, so polling more than once a minute gains nothing. A sensible client polls every one to two minutes and keeps its last good answer when a request fails.

chunks.title: API reference
chunks.text: Anonymous requests are limited to 60 a minute per IP address. Requests that carry an API key in Authorization: Bearer <key> are counted against the key instead, at 600 a minute. Windows are fixed one-minute windows. An unknown or revoked key answers 401. Every response also states the limit in force, so a client can read it rather than hard-code it: X-RateLimit-Limit (success): Requests allowed per minute: 60 anonymous, 600 with a Free key, more on a paid plan. X-RateLimit-Remaining (success): Requests left in it. Retry-After (429): Seconds to wait before trying again. Need more? Get a free key, instantly. A key on a paid plan gets that plan’s higher limit; see Plans & alerts.

chunks.title: API reference
chunks.text: Errors are JSON with a single error string. 400 (history: chain or ticker malformed): Check the parameters. Body: {"error":"chain and ticker"}. 400 (movers: window, limit, chain or ticker malformed): Use window=1h or 24h, a limit from 1 to 50, and a ticker only with a chain. 405 (a method other than GET or OPTIONS): Use GET. 401 (unknown or revoked API key): Check the key, or request one at app.gullylabs.xyz. 403 (history: days beyond what your plan includes): Ask for fewer days, or move to a plan with more history. The body names your limit in historyDays. 429 (rate limit exceeded): Wait for Retry-After seconds, or use an API key. 502 (the tracker could not be built at all): Retry in a minute. A partial failure is not a 502: it shows as unreadable rows.

chunks.title: Widget guide
chunks.text: Two themes, dark and light. Gaps outside the in-line band are teal above fair and vermilion below; in-line gaps and thin pools stay neutral. Ticker and table fill the width of their element; a badge is at most 340 px wide. Size the element to size the widget. Below 360 px the table drops its fair column so nothing is cut off. The widget draws inside its own shadow root, so your CSS does not reach in and its CSS does not leak out. The outer box is exposed as a part: [data-gully-widget]::part(widget) can set its border radius or shadow.

chunks.title: Widget guide
chunks.text: One request to the API per page, however many widgets share it, repeated every 60 seconds. If a refresh fails, the last good figures stay on screen and the footer reads “last read” instead of “live”. Before the first answer the widget says it is reading; if that fails, it says so and retries every minute. Errors stay inside the widget. Nothing is thrown into your page. Widgets added after the page loads, for example by a single-page app, are picked up automatically. window.GullyWidget.scan() forces a scan. Under prefers-reduced-motion the ticker stops scrolling and becomes a strip you can scroll by hand. Every widget carries a small “Gully Labs tracker” link to the live tracker. It is part of the free embed and stays. The widget never sends an API key and should not: anything in a page’s HTML is public. Its requests are anonymous and edge-cached. For heavier use, call the API from your server with a key.

chunks.text: The API is open without a key. A key raises your rate limit and counts your requests against your own allowance instead of your IP address. When you need a Gully Labs API key, how to get one instantly by signing in with a wallet, how to send it as a Bearer token, and how rate limits are reported.

chunks.title: API keys
chunks.text: Not for the widget: it is anonymous and shares one cached request per page. Not for trying the API, or for a page that reads it once a minute. Yes for a backend, bot or app that calls the API often, or from shared infrastructure where many callers share one IP address.

chunks.title: API keys
chunks.text: Keys are free and issued instantly at app.gullylabs.xyz. There is no form and no approval: Press Connect wallet and pick any browser wallet or Coinbase Wallet. Your wallet address is your account; there is no email or password. Sign the message your wallet shows. It is Sign-In with Ethereum (EIP-4361): a signature, not a transaction, so it costs nothing and moves nothing. It names app.gullylabs.xyz, expires after ten minutes and can be used once. Open API keys, press Create key and name it. The key works at once. Copy it then: it is shown in full only once, because we store only a hash of it. Smart-contract wallets (EIP-1271, including ones not deployed yet, ERC-6492) are accepted on Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain and Robinhood Chain. A sign-in lasts 30 days on that browser.

chunks.title: API keys
chunks.text: A wallet can hold up to five live keys. Each has its own 600-a-minute allowance. Rotate gives a key a new secret and stops the old one immediately; its name and usage history stay. Revoke stops a key for good. The dashboard shows requests per hour or day for each key, the error rate, and the last 50 requests with status and latency. Answers served from the edge cache never reach our servers and are not counted. A key issued through the earlier request form keeps working. Link it to your wallet from the API keys page to manage it there.

chunks.title: API keys
chunks.text: Every successful response carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining. Past the limit the API answers 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds. Today that is 60 requests a minute per IP address without a key and 600 a minute with one; read the headers rather than hard-coding either, because they can change. Details in the API reference. The data refreshes about every two minutes, so polling more often than once a minute returns the same answer.

chunks.title: API keys
chunks.text: Keep the key on a server or in an environment variable. Anything shipped to a browser, an app bundle or a public repository is public. Do not put a key in the widget snippet: the widget does not read one. If a key is exposed, rotate or revoke it on the developers dashboard; the old secret stops working at once. To serve many browser users, call the API from your server with your key and cache the answer for a minute. Your users then never touch the limit.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: The API stays free. Paid plans raise the per-key rate limit, add gap alerts and keep a longer history. You pay in ETH, BNB, USDC or USDT from your own wallet straight to ours. Paid plans for the Gully Labs tracker API, paid in USDC, USDT or the chain's own coin on Base, Ethereum, BNB Chain, Arbitrum, OP Mainnet, Polygon or Avalanche with no custody; gap alerts by webhook or Telegram; the webhook payload and how to verify its signature.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: A plan belongs to your wallet account and applies to every key it holds. The limits below are read live from GET /api/plans, the same source the pricing page and the dashboard use.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: Prices are in US dollars. You pay in USDC, USDT or the chain's own coin (ETH, BNB, POL, AVAX) on Base, Ethereum, BNB Chain, Arbitrum, OP Mainnet, Polygon or Avalanche, straight to the Gully Labs treasury wallet, which is the same address on every chain. The treasury is a Safe, so a chain is offered only once the Safe is deployed there; the list below is the live one. Open Plan & billing on the app dashboard, choose a plan, then a chain and an asset. You get a quote: the exact amount to send and the treasury address, valid for 20 minutes. Stablecoins count one to one with the dollar; the quote adds a few millionths as a tag. ETH and BNB are priced by the Chainlink USD feed on the same chain at the moment of the quote and rounded up, with a unique tail in the last digits. The quote shows the feed, its round and when it last updated. If the feed is more than two hours old, no quote is given in that coin. Press Pay with a wallet for a one-click transfer (the wallet is asked to switch to the quote’s chain), or send the amount from any wallet or exchange and paste the transaction hash.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: a wallet for a one-click transfer (the wallet is asked to switch to the quote’s chain), or send the amount from any wallet or exchange and paste the transaction hash. The server reads the receipt and the transaction from a public node of that chain and checks that they agree. A payment counts when it succeeded, is on the quote’s chain, paid the treasury in the quoted asset, has the confirmations above, and its hash was never used before on any chain. The plan starts the moment it is confirmed. From the wallet you signed in with, at least the price counts: any stablecoin amount from the dollar price up, or at least the quoted amount of ETH or BNB (paying more is accepted, paying less is refused and says by how much). From any other wallet or an exchange, send the exact quoted amount: its last digits tag the payment as yours, so nobody watching the treasury can claim it. A coin payment must be mined while its quote holds (ten minutes of grace). A payment buys days. Paying again for the same plan adds them to the end; a different plan starts that day. Nothing renews by itself: to cancel, don’t pay again. When a plan lapses you are back on Free and your keys keep working at the Free limit.

The payment goes straight to the treasury wallet in your own transfer. We hold no balance and no card, and nothing leaves your wallet unless you sign it. chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: GET /api/tracker/history takes days, up to what your plan includes. Without it the answer is the last seven days, unchanged. Asking for more than your plan includes answers 403 with your limit in historyDays. History is what the tracker recorded since long-term storage began; days before that are simply absent, never filled in.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: An alert watches one stock (chain and ticker) or every stock the tracker follows, for one condition: gap ({ type: "gap", pct, direction }): The gap between on-chain and fair price is at least pct percent. direction picks the side: above a premium (gap ≥ +pct), below a discount (gap ≤ −pct), or both (the default, and what alerts made before directions read as). status ({ type: "status", status }): The tracker flags the stock premium, discount, or either. Alerts are checked on every tracker snapshot, every five minutes. Per stock, an alert fires when its condition becomes true and re-arms once it is false again. It does not repeat while the condition simply stays true. Each alert sends at most one delivery every 30 minutes. Stocks that trigger during that pause go out with the next delivery if their condition still holds. Only rows the tracker would itself flag count: a readable feed and pool, a pool deep enough to flag, a fresh pool read and an open feed session. Anything else neither fires nor re-arms. Each delivery is logged in the dashboard with its HTTP status (the last 50 per alert). Use Test to send an alert.test delivery with no events. When a plan lapses, the alerts beyond the Free allowance stay listed but are paused until you delete some or upgrade; the oldest ones keep running.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: A second kind of alert watches DeepCore, the launchpad and DEX in the Gully Labs family, for new token launches. It has no stock: it watches one DeepCore chain, or every chain when chainId is left empty. deepcore-launch ({ type: "deepcore-launch", chainId }): A token launches on DeepCore on that chain: 56 BNB Chain, 999 HyperEVM, 4663 Robinhood Chain or 8453 Base; null for any of them. DeepCore’s public API (GET /v1/launches) is read every 90 seconds. Each launch fires once, the first time it is seen; after a restart nothing already seen is sent again. Only launches made after the alert was created count (with an hour of slack for indexer lag), so a new alert does not replay the backlog. One delivery at most every 5 minutes per alert: launches seen in the meantime wait and go out together, up to the 20 most recent. A paused, muted or over-the-plan alert neither sends nor queues: launches it missed are not sent later. It counts against your plan’s alerts like a gap alert, and delivers the same way: webhook, Telegram or both, signed the same way (see below). When DeepCore cannot be read, nothing fires and nothing is invented; the next good read catches up on launches it has not seen.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: both, signed the same way (see below). When DeepCore cannot be read, nothing fires and nothing is invented; the next good read catches up on launches it has not seen. In Telegram, anyone can ask the bot /launches for the five latest DeepCore launches on every chain, or /launches base (also bsc, robinhood, hyperevm, or a chain id) for one chain. It reads the same 90-second cache as the alerts, says when the list is older because DeepCore could not be read, and names any chain DeepCore itself could not read. Launch information is not advice.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: We POST JSON with these headers: Content-Type: application/json, X-Gully-Timestamp (Unix seconds) and X-Gully-Signature (sha256= and the hex HMAC). Answer with any 2xx within 5 seconds; we do not follow redirects and do not retry, and the status is shown in your delivery log.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: The signature is HMAC-SHA256 with the alert’s secret over `${timestamp}.${rawBody}`. The secret (whsec_…) is shown once when you create the alert; New secret replaces it. Compare in constant time and refuse old timestamps. Webhook URLs must be https:// on a public address. The host is resolved before every delivery and private, loopback, link-local and other reserved addresses are refused. See API keys for keeping secrets out of browser code; the same applies here.

chunks.title: Plans & alerts
chunks.text: An alert can message a Telegram chat as well as, or instead of, calling a webhook. In the Alerts tab of the dashboard press Connect Telegram: it opens the bot with a one-time code (ten minutes, single use) that links the chat to your wallet account, so there is no chat id to copy. Add to a group does the same for a group; only the person who linked a group can unlink it. Then tick Telegram on any alert. Each message names the stock and chain, the gap, the on-chain and fair prices, the status and the pool liquidity, with a link to the stock page. Open NVDA opens the stock page; Mute 24h pauses that alert, on every channel, for 24 hours. Resume in the dashboard ends a mute early. Deliveries appear in the alert's log like webhook ones, with the result Telegram gave. In the chat, /alerts lists your alerts and /stop unlinks. Anyone can ask the bot /gap NVDA (or /gap NVDA bsc) and /top for the five widest trusted gaps. A figure the tracker could not read is said to be unreadable, never shown as zero. Which channels the server offers is public at GET /api/alerts/channels.

chunks.title: Teams & workspaces
chunks.text: Every wallet account is a workspace. Invite teammates by wallet or by link, give each a role, and see who changed what. Share one Gully Labs developer account with a team: workspaces, roles and what each may change, invites by wallet or by link, the activity log and CSV exports of usage and payments.

chunks.title: Teams & workspaces
chunks.text: When a wallet first signs in to the app dashboard, it gets its own workspace and is its owner. Everything in the portal belongs to the workspace: API keys, gap and DeepCore launch alerts, the linked Telegram chat, Gully Analytics, the plan and its payments. Members share all of it; nothing is copied per person. The workspace is named after its owner (0x1234…abcd’s workspace) until an admin or the owner renames it. A workspace holds at most 25 people, the owner included, and 20 open invites at a time. Membership is checked on every request. A member who is removed is moved back to their own workspace on their next request. If the owner’s wallet is blocked, the workspace is unavailable to every member.

chunks.title: Teams & workspaces
chunks.text: Every member can see everything in the workspace. A role decides what they may change: owner (everything): The wallet that owns the workspace. Cannot be removed or demoted, and is the only one who can add, change or remove admins. admin (keys, alerts, Telegram, Gully Analytics, billing, company details, the team): Invites and manages developers, billing members and viewers, and renames the workspace. developer (keys, alerts, Telegram, Gully Analytics): Creates, renames, rotates and revokes keys; manages alerts and analytics websites; can open Gully Analytics in one click (see single sign-on). Cannot pay or manage the team. billing (billing, company details): Buys and renews plans (tracker API and Gully Analytics) and keeps the invoice details current. viewer (nothing): Read-only: keys (prefixes only), usage, alerts, billing and the activity log. Your own profile, your sign-in sessions, switching workspace, leaving one and accepting an invite are open to every role. A request beyond your role answers 403 with {"code":"forbidden-role"}.

chunks.title: Teams & workspaces
chunks.text: Owners and admins invite from the Team tab, in two ways: By wallet. Enter the teammate’s address. The invite waits for that wallet: they sign in to the portal and accept it there. Nobody else can use it. By link. The portal makes a link (https://app.gullylabs.xyz/#invite=…) that anyone who signs in with a wallet can accept, once. The link is shown once; only a hash of it is kept, so it cannot be shown again. Send it privately. Every invite carries the role it grants and expires after 7 days. Accepted, revoked and expired invites stop working at once. Open invites can be revoked from the Team tab. Only the owner can invite, or revoke the invite of, an admin. Opening a link shows the workspace name, the role and who invited you before you accept. Unknown links and repeated attempts are rate limited per address. Owners and admins change a member’s role or remove them from the Team tab. Removing someone moves their sessions back to their own workspace, which is untouched.

chunks.title: Teams & workspaces
chunks.text: If you belong to more than one workspace, the portal’s workspace switcher lists yours first, then the others by name. The choice is kept for that sign-in session only, so two browsers can work in two workspaces. Members can leave a workspace from the Team tab; the owner cannot leave their own.

chunks.title: Teams & workspaces
chunks.text: The Activity tab lists who did what in the workspace, newest first, 50 at a time. It records: Keys: key.created, key.renamed, key.rotated, key.revoked, key.linked. Alerts and Telegram: alert.created, alert.updated, alert.tested, alert.deleted, telegram.linked, telegram.unlinked. Billing and analytics: billing.quote, billing.paid, analytics.trial, analytics.site_added, analytics.site_removed, analytics.password_reset, analytics.quote, analytics.plan. Team and account: team.invited, team.invite_revoked, team.joined, team.role_changed, team.removed, team.left, workspace.renamed, company.updated, profile.updated, sessions.revoked. Usage: usage.threshold, by system, when the workspace’s busiest key passes 80% or 100% of the plan’s per-minute limit (at most once a day per threshold). The owner can also have it sent to Telegram from their profile. Only successful changes are logged, and never a secret. A workspace keeps its newest 1,000 events and nothing older than 180 days. Reading it from code Page backwards by passing the previous page’s nextCursor as ?cursor=. A cursor that has aged out answers 400: start again from the first page.

chunks.title: Teams & workspaces
chunks.text: Two downloads from the portal, for whatever workspace is active. Any member, viewers included, can download them. usage.csv (one per time bucket and key): Requests made with the workspace’s keys: hourly buckets for 24h and 7d, daily (UTC) for 30d. client_err is 4xx other than 429, limited is 429, server_err is 5xx. payments.csv (one per payment, oldest first): Every payment for the workspace’s plans (tracker API and Gully Analytics), with the asset, chain, transaction hash and an explorer link. Every text cell that starts with =, +, -, @, a tab or a carriage return gets a leading ', so a spreadsheet shows it as text instead of running it as a formula. Cells with commas, quotes or line breaks are quoted. Files are UTF-8 with CRLF line ends.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: Who really holds a token: the biggest wallets as bubbles, the ones that trade with each other in gold, and a plain check of every DeepCore launch. How the Holder Map works: data sources per chain, clusters and hidden links, the launch health score part by part, live mode, alerts, the API and the honesty rules.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: The Holder Map covers two kinds of token: DeepCore launches and the stock tokens the tracker follows. Open one at gullylabs.xyz/holders by address or ticker, from a stock page, or from a launch in the Telegram bot. Every bubble is a wallet, sized by its share of the total supply (or of the listed holders when the supply could not be read; the map says which). Grey bubbles are not people: trading pools, liquidity and token locks, burn addresses, the token’s own contract, DeepCore and Gully Labs contracts, and exchanges. They are never put in a cluster and never counted in the “top 10 wallets” figure. The summary line says how much the top 10 wallets hold and how much the largest connected cluster holds, across how many wallets. A few plain sentences follow it. For stock tokens the map also shows what the top wallets hold at the real share price, and whether they sit on a premium or a discount to it.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: The map reads each chain from the cheapest source that is complete. A chain without its source says “holder data is not available on this chain yet”; it never shows an empty or made-up map. DeepCore launches (BNB Chain, HyperEVM, Robinhood Chain, Base) (DeepCore’s own log index: every transfer since the launch, so balances are exact): Every transfer between mapped wallets since the launch Stock tokens on Robinhood Chain (Blockscout’s API (top holders)): The latest transfers, read from the chain Stock tokens on BNB Chain (Moralis (top holders)): The latest transfers from Moralis Stock tokens on Solana (The Solana RPC (the 20 largest token accounts, merged by owner)): Not read on Solana yet Labels come from DeepCore’s list of its own contracts, the launch’s lock, the Gully Pay fee proxies, the tracker’s pool and public name tags (exchanges among them) from Blockscout’s metadata service.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: Two mapped wallets are linked when one sent the token to the other. Linked wallets form a cluster, drawn in kit gold (the largest) or pale gold. A cluster is often one person or team spread across many wallets, but not always: read it as a reason to look closer, not as proof. A hidden link joins two mapped wallets through an address that is not on the map (it passed tokens between them). It is drawn as a small hollow node with dashed lines; its tooltip names the address. For DeepCore launches the deployer’s funding of other wallets is a link too.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: Every DeepCore launch gets a score from 0 to 100, made of parts you can read one by one: whether the launch liquidity is locked, bundled buying in the first block of trading, snipers in the first blocks, the deployer’s share now, how much the top 10 wallets hold, and the deployer’s record of earlier launches. Each part shows its weight, the points it earned, the figure behind it and a plain reason. Tap a part on the map to light up the wallets behind it. The score, its parts, the bundled and deployer warnings and the liquidity check are never behind a plan. A part that could not be read is left out of the score and marked “not known”; it is never counted as good or bad. The card says how many parts were counted. The weights are the server’s: the API returns each part’s weight and points, so what the page shows is what was scored. The deployer’s record lists their other DeepCore launches with what happened to each (still trading, liquidity pulled, deployer sold, unknown). A deployer with many launches is marked “Serial launcher”. Wallets of the largest cluster that also hold other launches are listed under “Same wallets elsewhere”, with links to those maps.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: On a launch’s map page, live mode reads new transfers every 15 seconds: each one flows as a particle from sender to receiver (addresses that are not on the map come in from the edge), bubbles resize to the new shares, and a LIVE pill shows when the map last updated. Under reduced motion the particles are still lines that fade. The replay slider rebuilds holdings at earlier moments from the token’s own transfers: press play (1× or 4×) to watch holdings concentrate or spread since the launch.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: “Alert me” on a map opens the Alerts tab of the app with the token filled in. Pick what to watch (the largest cluster, the top 10, or the deployer’s share) and a threshold; deliveries go to Telegram and webhooks like every other alert, and count towards your plan’s alerts. See Plans & alerts.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: GET /api/holders/:chain/:token answers the whole map as JSON;.csv gives the holder list and /card.png a share card. Requests count against the same keys and limits as the tracker. Field by field: API reference. To put a map on your own page, use the widget script with data-gully-widget="holders": see the widget guide.

chunks.title: Holder Map
chunks.text: Nothing is estimated or typed in: every figure is read from the sources above, with the time it was read. A value that could not be read is shown as such, never as zero. Labels name only what a source says an address is. The map is information, not advice. Clusters and scores are signals to look closer, not verdicts on a person.

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: Privacy-friendly web analytics with Web3 tracking for dapps: page views plus wallet connects, chain switches and transactions. It is a fork of Umami; everything Umami does still works. Gully Analytics: sign up with a wallet, install the tracker, Web3 events, address privacy modes, plans and what happens at the quota or when a plan lapses.

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: Open the app dashboard, connect a wallet and sign the sign-in message (no transaction, no gas). In the Analytics tab press Start free trial. The server creates a Gully Analytics login for your wallet and shows its password once; copy it. We do not keep the password. Reset password in the same tab sets a new one and signs out open sessions. Add a website with its name and domain. The tab shows its website id, the install snippet, a link to its dashboard and the events counted this month. The free trial runs once per wallet. After it, choose a plan in the same tab to keep recording.

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: The quickest way in is Open Gully Analytics in the Analytics tab of the app dashboard. It signs you straight in to the dashboard, with no password to type: the portal asks the server for a one-time sign-in link (POST /api/developer/analytics/sso), and the browser opens it on analytics.gullylabs.xyz. The link works once and only for 60 seconds, from the browser that asked for it. Only a hash of it is kept. Owners, admins and developers of the workspace can use it; billing members and viewers cannot. Everyone in the workspace opens the same Gully Analytics account. It never shows, changes or resets the account’s password, so a password you saved keeps working. The password login at analytics.gullylabs.xyz/login still works for anyone with the password. Forgot it? Reset password in the portal’s Analytics tab sets a new one.

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: Put the snippet on every page, before the closing head tag. The Analytics tab gives it with your website id filled in. Without data-web3="true" the script behaves exactly like the Umami tracker. The usual Umami attributes (data-domains, data-do-not-track, data-tag, data-before-send, …) still apply, and Web3 events respect them.

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: The script finds wallets through EIP-6963 and window.ethereum and watches what your dapp asks of them. It never calls a wallet method itself, so it cannot trigger a wallet prompt. All four events are standard custom events with event data, so they also show under Events, Goals, Funnels and filters. chainId is a decimal number; wallet is the wallet’s EIP-6963 id (io.metamask, io.rabby, …) or its name. You can send these events yourself too, and the Web3 dashboard reads them the same:

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: data-web3-address decides what is stored about the wallet address: hash (default) (counted): The first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the lowercase address. Wallets can be counted; the address cannot be read back. full (counted): The lowercase address. none (not counted): Nothing. Unique wallets and transactions per wallet show 0 or a dash. Hashing needs a secure context (HTTPS or localhost); on plain HTTP the address is dropped rather than sent in clear. A hash of a public address is pseudonymous, not anonymous: anyone with a candidate address can hash it and compare. Use none if that matters for your users.

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: The plans below are read live from GET /api/plans (field analytics), the same source the pricing page and the dashboard use. An event is any call the tracker makes for one of your websites: page views, custom events and Web3 events. They are counted across your websites per calendar month in UTC. At the limit, new events are not recorded until the month turns or you upgrade. The tracker gets an HTTP 402 answer and stops sending for the rest of that page view. Websites beyond what your plan includes (after a downgrade, say) do not record until you remove some or upgrade; the oldest ones keep recording. Paying works like the tracker API plans (see Paying): USDC, USDT or the chain's own coin on Base, Ethereum, BNB Chain, Arbitrum, OP Mainnet, Polygon or Avalanche (where the treasury is deployed), straight to the treasury, checked on chain. A payment buys days; paying again for the same plan adds them to the end. Nothing renews by itself. When a trial or plan ends, recording stops. Your dashboard stays readable for days; after that the account and its data may be deleted.

chunks.title: Gully Analytics
chunks.text: Sign in at analytics.gullylabs.xyz with the login from the Analytics tab. Each website has the usual Umami views plus a Web3 tab: unique wallets, connects, connect rate, transactions, transactions per wallet, a visit → connect → transaction funnel, chains, wallet apps and the top pages by connects. The Umami REST API works with your own login: sign in with POST /api/auth/login and send the token as Authorization: Bearer …. The Web3 figures are at GET /api/websites/{websiteId}/web3?startAt=…&endAt=…. The source is public: gully-labs/umami, MIT licensed like Umami.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: Non-custodial crypto billing: every payment is a plain transfer from the payer’s wallet straight to the treasury, read back from the chain. Invoices, reusable pay links, a hosted checkout and signed webhooks. Gully Pay: invoices and reusable pay links in USDC, USDT or the chain's own coin on seven chains, wallet QR codes, the Pay with crypto button, and signed merchant webhooks with how to verify them.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: An invoice (/pay/inv_…) asks for one US dollar amount. The payer picks a chain and an asset and gets a quote: the exact amount to send, valid for 20 minutes. Stablecoins count one to one with a unique tag in the last digits; the chains' own coins (ETH, BNB, POL, AVAX) are priced by the Chainlink USD feed on the same chain. A payment is checked on chain (success, right chain, right asset, the treasury, the exact amount, enough confirmations, never used before) before the invoice is marked paid. The same rules as API plans apply. Base (8453) (10): USDC (6 decimals), ETH Ethereum (1) (6): USDC, USDT (6 decimals), ETH BNB Chain (56) (15): USDT, USDC (18 decimals), BNB Arbitrum (42161) (10): USDC (6 decimals), ETH OP Mainnet (10) (10): USDC, USDT (6 decimals), ETH Polygon (137) (64): USDC (6 decimals), POL Avalanche (43114) (2): USDC, USDT (6 decimals), AVAX The live list, read from GET /api/plans as you look at this page (hover a chain for its assets and confirmations): Nothing is held in between: the transfer goes to the treasury in the payer’s own transaction. If no treasury is configured, every page says checkout is closed and shows no amount or QR.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: The treasury is a Safe: the same address on every chain, but it only exists on a chain where it has been deployed. The server reads eth_getCode(treasury) on every chain at start and hourly; a chain where the treasury has no code is not offered (no quote, no pay link, no checkout, no QR) until the Safe is deployed there, when it switches on by itself. The live list above is already filtered this way. Merchant payments go to the merchant's own wallet (checked the same way, per chain). The Gully Pay fee on a stablecoin payment is collected inside that payment through Request Network's ERC20FeeProxy only on a chain where that contract is verified byte for byte and the treasury is deployed; everywhere else, and for coin payments, the payer makes one plain transfer and the fee is invoiced to the merchant weekly. The payer never sees a difference in the amount. Base (proxy verified (0x1892…b814) · treasury deployed): stablecoins: one approve + one call pays merchant and fee; coins: one transfer Ethereum (proxy verified (0x370D…623C) · treasury deployed): same as Base BNB Chain (proxy verified (0x0Dfb…0aC9) · treasury deployed): same as Base Arbitrum (proxy verified (0x0Dfb…0aC9) · treasury deployed): same as Base OP Mainnet (proxy verified, byte-identical to Base (0x399F…cbfE) · treasury not deployed yet): Gully Labs checkout: not offered until the Safe is deployed there. Stores: one transfer, fee invoiced; once the Safe is deployed, same as Base

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: (0x399F…cbfE) · treasury not deployed yet): Gully Labs checkout: not offered until the Safe is deployed there. Stores: one transfer, fee invoiced; once the Safe is deployed, same as Base Polygon (proxy present (0x0Dfb…0aC9) but a different build from Base’s: not used · treasury not deployed yet): Gully Labs checkout: not offered until the Safe is deployed there. Stores: one transfer, fee invoiced Avalanche (proxy present (0x0Dfb…0aC9) but a different build from Base’s: not used · treasury not deployed yet): Gully Labs checkout: not offered until the Safe is deployed there. Stores: one transfer, fee invoiced Solana (no Request deployment · its own treasury (GULLY_SOLANA_TREASURY)): one Solana Pay transfer; a merchant fee is invoiced Each new chain's proxy was read with eth_getCode through three or more public RPCs and its runtime, metadata stripped, compared with Base's 0x1892…b814; only a byte-identical one is used for a split (OP Mainnet). Polygon's and Avalanche's are other builds of the same source, so those chains stay on plain transfers with the fee invoiced. The addresses, hashes and what each RPC answered are in contracts/CHOICE.md. GET /api/plans carries feeProxy (verified contract exists) and feeSplit (usable now) per chain.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: A pay link (/pay/l/pl_…, an unguessable id) is reusable: every payer who opens it gets an invoice of their own, linked back to the link, then lands in the checkout. Links are made in the admin dashboard. title, description (string): Shown on the link, the checkout and the receipt. amount (fixed | open): A fixed USD amount, or open: the payer types an amount between a minimum and a maximum. The server checks it; the page cannot change it. assets (string[]): Which chain and asset pairs it takes (all by default). active (boolean): Switched off links take no payments. expiresAt (date | null): After it, the link takes no payments. maxUses (number | null): How many paid uses it allows. Checkouts in progress count against it, so a one-off link cannot be paid twice. webhook (https URL | null): Where its events go (webhooks). An invoice made from a link stays open for an hour. Its quote holds 20 minutes and can be renewed. Each address may start ten checkouts from links an hour. A switched-off, expired or used-up link says so plainly and starts no checkout.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: Title, amount and a status pill: awaiting payment, confirming, paid, expired or cancelled. Assets grouped by chain; the exact amount, large; a wallet QR; copy buttons for the amount, the treasury address and the token contract. A countdown on the quote, and a new quote when it runs out. A payment sent in time can still be checked after. Pay with wallet sends the exact transfer from a connected wallet. Or send from anywhere and paste the transaction hash. Live confirmations (n / needed), then a receipt with the explorer link, ready to print or save as PDF.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: Stablecoin payments to a store carry Gully Labs’ fee in the same transaction through Request Network’s ERC20FeeProxy, an immutable contract with no owner. It never holds tokens: one call moves the payment from the payer to the recipient and the fee to the treasury, and returns. The only way funds could end up inside it is a transfer sent straight to the proxy’s address, and nobody, Gully Labs included, could get those back. So the server and the checkout make that impossible: Every quote, QR code, wallet link, recipient address and split call passes one validator before it leaves the server. A proxy address (on any chain) is never a recipient; a split calls the proxy only through transferFromWithReferenceAndFee with zero value, an allowed stablecoin, the recipient and the treasury as the two legs and an approval for exactly the amount. Anything else answers 500 with no payment details at all. The Pay with wallet button checks the same rules again in the browser, simulates the proxy call with eth_call before your wallet sees it, and refuses to send on any failure. It never sends coin to the proxy and never falls back to a plain transfer to it. An hourly monitor reads every proxy’s balances on every chain. A non-zero balance (a transfer someone sent to the proxy by hand) alerts the Gully Labs team, who cannot recover it either but can warn the payer. Pay with the wallet button or send to the address shown on the quote. Never copy the pay.to contract address of a split into a wallet as a recipient: a plain transfer to it is lost for good, and the server names such a transaction as an unrecoverable mis-send instead of a payment.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: Every quote carries an uri: an EIP-681 payment request for the exact amount, built on the server from base units (never floating point). The QR encodes it. Wallet support for EIP-681 varies: some read only the address, some ignore the amount or the chain. The checkout always shows the address, the exact amount and the token contract with copy buttons. Check the amount and the network in the wallet before sending.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: Paste this on any site to send buyers to a pay link or an invoice. The link alone opens the checkout in a new tab; the optional script opens it in a popup window. The admin shows the snippet for each link and invoice. The checkout cannot be put in an iframe: its pages send frame-ancestors limited to Gully Labs itself, so wallet prompts and the address bar stay visible to the payer.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: A pay link, an invoice, or a default endpoint for everything else can have a webhook. When an invoice has its own, or its link has one, events go there; otherwise to the default, if set. invoice.paid (The payment is confirmed and the invoice marked paid.): invoice, link, payment invoice.expired (An open invoice ran out without a payment.): invoice, link invoice.cancelled (Gully Labs cancelled the invoice; it can no longer be paid. A cancelled invoice never sends invoice.expired afterwards.): invoice, link webhook.test (The admin pressed Send test event.): target, message https only. No user name or password in the URL. The host must resolve only to public addresses: private, loopback, link-local and reserved ranges are refused, and the request goes to the address that was checked. The signing secret (whsec_…) is shown once, when the endpoint is set. Rotating it shows the new one once; the old one stops at once. Five-second timeout, redirects not followed, the response body is not read.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: Every request carries two headers. The signature is an HMAC-SHA256, with your secret, of the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body: X-Gully-Timestamp (unix seconds): When it was sent. Refuse old ones (five minutes) to stop replays. X-Gully-Signature (sha256=<hex>): hex(HMAC-SHA256(secret, `${timestamp}.${rawBody}`)) It is the same scheme as gap alerts, so one verifier serves both.

chunks.title: Gully Pay
chunks.text: The first attempt goes out at once. Any answer other than 2xx, a timeout or a network error is retried after 1, 5, 10, 20 and 30 minutes: six attempts over about an hour. Then the delivery is marked failed. Retries carry the same event id and body; each is signed again with the current secret and timestamp. The queue is stored on disk, so a restart loses nothing: attempts that came due while the server was down go out when it is back. Each link and invoice shows its delivery log in the admin: event, state, attempts, last answer. A finished delivery (failed or delivered) can be redelivered from the admin, for example after your endpoint was down for longer than the retries. The same event goes out again, with the same id and body, as a new delivery with its own six attempts. Your handler should already drop an id it has handled. Events may arrive out of order and, rarely, more than once. Treat invoice.paid as the source of truth for a sale and look the invoice up by id.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: Take USDC, USDT and the chains' own coins on Base, Ethereum, BNB Chain, Arbitrum, OP Mainnet, Polygon and Avalanche, straight into your own wallet. Non-custodial: payments go directly to your wallet. Gully Labs never holds your funds. Run your own non-custodial crypto checkout: wallets per chain, pay links and invoices, signed webhooks, a transaction fee only, weekly statements and the pause policy.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: Every workspace in the app dashboard can be a store. Open the Merchant tab (app.gullylabs.xyz/#merchant), add a receiving wallet and name the store: from then on your pay links and invoices take payments. The checkout, quotes and on-chain checks are the same as Gully Pay uses for Gully Labs itself; the only difference is where the money goes: your wallet. The payer sends a plain transfer from their wallet to yours, in their own transaction. We read it back from a public node of that chain. Nothing passes through an account of ours, and we cannot move, hold or refund a payment.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: Wallets: one address per chain (the same address on every chain is fine). Store profile: name, logo (https, PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, 256 KB at most; fetched once and served from our origin), accent colour, support email and website. They head every checkout, which ends with “Powered by Gully Pay”. Roles: owners, admins and billing members run the store (wallets, profile, invoices); developers make pay links and set the webhook; viewers read everything.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: A mixed-case address must match its EIP-55 checksum exactly, so a mistyped character cannot slip through. An all-lower-case (or all-upper-case) address carries no checksum: it is accepted and stored in its checksummed form. We read the chain: an address with no code is a wallet (EOA); with code, a contract (a Safe or another smart account); an EIP-7702 delegated EOA is shown as such. A contract must be deployed on a chain before that chain can be turned on. A Safe's address can exist on a chain before the Safe is deployed there; a payment to it then may be lost. If you say the wallet is a contract, or it is a contract on another of our chains, and it has no code on this one, the chain stays off. Deploy it, then press Check again, or leave it: we read every undeployed wallet again each hour, and the chain switches on by itself once the contract is there (unless you turned it off). Gully Labs' own treasury cannot be a store wallet. Never a fee proxy contract. Request Network's ERC20FeeProxy (the contract a split payment passes through) has no owner: anything sent straight to its address is lost for good. The form and the server both refuse it as a store wallet, and you should never give its address to a customer as a place to pay. Your customers pay your wallet; the proxy only passes the payment through inside one transaction.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.section: Using a Safe as your store wallet
chunks.text: A Safe (the multisig from safe.global) is a good store wallet: several owners, a threshold, no single key. One thing to know: a Safe exists only on the chains where it was deployed. Its address is the same everywhere, but on a chain where nobody deployed it there is no contract behind it, and a payment sent there is lost. That is why a chain stays off until the Safe has code on it. Deploy Safe on <chain>. A wallet row that reads “not deployed” has this button. We read your Safe on a chain where it exists (owners, threshold, version), recover its creation transaction (the salt and the exact set-up call live only there: from a transaction you created through us, the first block it had code in, or Safe's own service, each verified), check that Safe's official factory, singleton and fallback handler are on the target chain with the expected code, and compute the address the factory call would create. Only if that address is exactly your Safe's do we offer the call; the page recomputes it once more before your wallet is asked. Your wallet signs. Connect any wallet with a little of the chain's coin for gas (about 240,000 gas; the estimate is shown first). It does not have to be a Safe owner. The transaction goes from your wallet to Safe's factory; Gully Labs never holds a key and never sends anything.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.section: Using a Safe as your store wallet
chunks.text: shown first). It does not have to be a Safe owner. The transaction goes from your wallet to Safe's factory; Gully Labs never holds a key and never sends anything. Sent → Mined → Verified. We read the receipt, then the code and owners at the address, and run the same check as “Check again”: the chain switches on by itself. The copy starts as the original was set up. If you added owners or changed the threshold after creating the Safe, the new chain starts with the original owners and threshold; change them there afterwards in Safe{Wallet}. Guards and modules are not copied. A Safe that paid for its own deployment, or whose set-up calls a contract missing on the target chain, is refused rather than deployed broken. No Safe yet? Create one. List the owners (your connected wallet is filled in), pick a threshold and a chain. We plan a Safe 1.4.1 from Safe's official factory with a deterministic salt we keep, so you see the address before anything is sent and can later deploy the same Safe at that address on every other chain with one click. Once verified it becomes your store wallet on that chain.

chunks.section: Using a Safe as your store wallet
chunks.text: anything is sent and can later deploy the same Safe at that address on every other chain with one click. Once verified it becomes your store wallet on that chain. What cannot be reproduced. Only Safe 1.3.0 and 1.4.1 from Safe's official factory. A Safe created with createProxy (plain CREATE, old 1.3.0 flows) or by another factory has an address that depends on that factory's own history: create a new Safe for that chain instead. The fee-proxy contracts and Gully Labs' treasury are never a target. Nothing in this flow holds money: the deployment transaction carries no value, the Safe is deployed by Safe's audited factory, and until the chain shows the code and owners the chain stays off and no checkout offers it.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: Pay link (/pay/m/l/ml_…): Title, description, a fixed amount or one the payer chooses between a minimum and a maximum, assets, optional expiry and maximum uses. Each payer gets an invoice of their own (open one hour). Invoice (/pay/m/mi_…): Number (INV-0001… or yours), line items, due date, customer name and email, notes, assets. Payable 30 days past the due date (shown overdue), then it expires. Each has a copy button, a QR code of its checkout URL and a “Pay with crypto” button snippet for your site (the same snippet and popup script as Gully Pay's own links).

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: Your name, logo and accent; the amount; for an invoice, the line items, who it is billed to and the due date; the wallet it pays on each chain. The payer picks a chain and an asset and gets a 20-minute quote for an exact amount (stablecoins 1:1 plus a tag in the last digits; ETH, BNB, POL and AVAX at the Chainlink price on that chain). A payment counts only when it sent your wallet exactly the quoted amount in the quoted asset on the quoted chain, inside the quote's time, with the chain's confirmations, and its transaction was never used for anything else, by you, another store or Gully Labs. A transfer to any other address never counts. Stablecoin payments above your free allowance pay your wallet and Gully Labs' fee in one transaction through Request Network's ERC20FeeProxy, which never holds funds. Every quote, QR code and split call is checked on the server (and again in the payer's browser, with a simulation) so that nothing ever names the proxy as a recipient; a payment that cannot pass answers with no payment details at all. Details in Funds can't get stuck.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: One https endpoint per store gets invoice.paid, invoice.expired and invoice.cancelled for your invoices and link checkouts, signed with your own secret (shown once, rotatable). The signing scheme, retries (six attempts over about an hour) and redeliver are Gully Pay's: see verifying the signature.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: A transaction fee only: no monthly fee, no set-up fee. Where the fee is collected depends on the chain (the checkout marks each chain, and your store's setup page lists them): Base, Ethereum, BNB Chain, Arbitrum (your wallet and the fee are paid in the same transaction (Request Network fee proxy, verified on each chain); the payer pays exactly the quoted amount): one transfer to your wallet; the fee is invoiced OP Mainnet (the proxy is verified there too (byte-identical to Base's); the in-payment fee switches on once Gully Labs' treasury is deployed on that chain, and until then the fee is invoiced): one transfer to your wallet; the fee is invoiced Polygon, Avalanche (one transfer to your wallet; the fee is invoiced (the fee proxy there is a different build from the one we verified, so it is not used)): one transfer to your wallet; the fee is invoiced Each workspace's first lifetime volume up to the free allowance is fee-free. A payment that crosses it pays only on the part above it. The fee accrues on each confirmed payment at its quoted USD value, exactly (in millionths of a dollar). Every Monday at 00:00 UTC, a store that owes $1 or more gets a statement: a normal Gully Labs invoice, payable in crypto through the Gully Pay checkout. Less than $1 rolls into the next week. The portal shows the balance, the free allowance left, every statement and a Pay now button. The CSV export lists every payment with its fee. The fee terms in full: section 5 of the merchant terms.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: Day 0: the statement is issued. You are told in the activity log and on Telegram if your workspace linked a chat. Day 5: a reminder. Day 7, still unpaid: your checkouts pause. Payers see “This store's checkout is paused” and no new quote or link checkout starts. A payment already sent against an earlier quote is still checked and recorded: the money is in your wallet either way. Paying the statement resumes checkout at once.

chunks.title: Gully Pay for merchants
chunks.text: Running a store means accepting the Gully Pay merchant terms (adapted from Common Paper's Cloud Service Agreement, CC BY 4.0): you tick “I agree” when you add your first receiving wallet.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: Scan contracts and code from the app, read the findings with their locations and draft proofs of concept, and ask people for a Security Review when a scan is not enough. Live today: the AI Security Scan, the Gully Score and contract monitors. Gully Security: the AI Security Scan (live; an AI review only for now), reading and publishing a report, the Gully Score and monitors, and requesting a human Security Review (quoted on request). Full audits are not offered.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: AI Security Scan (live): automated and self-serve, in the app. For now it is an AI review only: our static-tools worker is not running yet, so Slither, Aderyn and fuzzing do not run, and every report says so in its label and lists those tools as not run. The AI reads the code for known vulnerability classes and ranks what it finds. Security Review (on request): people read your code, check the findings by hand and write up what they find. Quoted per project after a request. Audit: planned for later. It is not offered today and cannot be requested yet. Gully Score and monitors (live): see the Gully Score and the Monitors tab of the app. A scan can miss issues (business logic, economic and cross-contract attacks, off-chain risks) and can report false positives. Every report says so. Gully Labs has not audited any project.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: Open the Security page of the app and follow the five steps: choose the input, confirm the scope and the cost, pay if the free quota is used up, watch it run, read the report. Deployed contract (address + chain): Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, OP Mainnet, Polygon, BNB Chain or Avalanche; the verified source is read from the chain. Smart contract repo (owner/name + commit): A public GitHub repository; leave the commit empty for the default branch (the report names the exact commit it scanned). Upload (.zip of Solidity files, or one.sol): Web2 repo (owner/name + commit): A JavaScript or TypeScript backend on GitHub: a checklist scan, not a penetration test. A scan moves through queued, fetching, analysing, triaging and reporting to done (or failed with the reason, or cancelled if you stop it). The app shows each step live with the engine's own step text and an estimate of the time left. You can leave the page; the scan keeps running. Asking for a target you are already scanning shows that scan instead of starting another.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: A paid scan gets a Gully Pay invoice, payable in the app or at its /pay/… page in USDC, USDT or the chain's own coin, straight to the Gully Labs treasury. The scan starts by itself once the payment is confirmed. If the price changes between your confirmation and the request (say a teammate used the last free scan), the app asks you to confirm again.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: The report's mode, shown as its label: static+ai (static tools plus AI triage), ai-only (“AI review only — static tools unavailable”), static-only, bytecode-only (source not verified) or checklist (web2). Findings by severity (critical, high, medium, low, info; severity is likelihood × impact) as a donut and bars; click one to filter the list. Each finding expands to its description, code location (file and line, with the snippet when the engine gives one), recommendation and status. A proof of concept where the engine could write one, labelled “Draft, not executed” unless the scanner ran it. Every finding is marked not verified by a human. The PoC code is visible to your workspace only. Every tool that ran, and every tool that did not, with the reason. Dismissed tool findings with the reason, the limitations of the scan and the disclaimer, verbatim. Export PDF opens the print-ready report in a new tab: print it or save it as PDF.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: The workspace owner or an admin can publish a finished report. It then lives at a stable address, /security/reports/sec_…, and in the list of published reports. Search engines are asked not to index it unless you also tick “Let search engines index it”. Unpublishing takes it down at once. The code of a proof of concept is never part of a public report (its status is), and neither is your workspace.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: Use the form on the Security page or under Request a review in the app. Tell us the project, what should be reviewed and, if you like, the repository, the contract and your timeline. We reply by email with questions or a quote; nothing is booked or charged by the form.

chunks.title: Gully Security
chunks.text: GET /api/developer/security (members): Free scans left, the offer, chains, engine state. GET /api/developer/security/scans (members): The workspace’s scans, newest first. POST /api/developer/security/scans (developer, admin, owner): { input, upload?, expect: { priceUsd } } → 201 started or 202 with an invoice. GET …/scans/:id, …/scans/:id/events (members): One scan with its report; live progress as Server-Sent Events. POST …/scans/:id/cancel (developer, admin, owner): Cancels before payment (and the invoice) or while running. POST …/scans/:id/publish (admin, owner): { published, indexable? } GET /api/security/reports[/:id] (anyone): Published reports only. POST /api/security/review-requests (anyone): A request for a Security Review (audits are not offered yet).

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: The Gully Score is a 0 to 100 reading of how a contract is controlled and how it has behaved, built only from public evidence. Every part is shown with its weight, its source, a plain reason and a link to the evidence. How the Gully Score is worked out: every component, its weight and source, what happens when data is missing, monitoring alerts, the badge and widget, and why nobody can pay to change a score.

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: Each contract has a public page at /score/<chain>/<address> on gullylabs.xyz/score, with the score, the parts that went into it, its history and a log of every change. A score is read again when it is more than six hours old, and soon after Gully Security monitoring sees a privileged change on the contract. Scores are informational. They are not an endorsement and not investment advice. A high score says the public evidence looks good; it does not say a contract is safe.

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: The weights below are read live from the score service, the same numbers every score page uses. The score is the weighted average of the parts that could be read. Code verified: an exact Sourcify match scores 100, a partial match 85, no published source 0. Who controls it: nobody (ownership given up) or a Safe needing two or more signatures 100, a timelock 80, an unrecognised contract 50, a Safe any one signer can use 40, a single wallet 15. Delay on changes: two days or more 100, one day 90, six hours 60, anything shorter 40, none 0. Can the code change: fixed code 100, upgradeable 30. Recent privileged changes: 100 less 25 for each change in the last 30 days. Liquidity locked: the share of the launch pools with a lock record, for DeepCore launches. Holder spread: the Holder Map’s Launch Health, or from the top-10 share (20% or less is 100, 90% or more is 0). Gully Security review: 100 less 40 per critical, 20 per high, 5 per medium and 1 per low finding (unresolved ones when the report says). Age: a year or more 100, six months 85, three months 70, a month 50, a week 30, younger 10.

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: When a part cannot be read (the contract is not verified anywhere we can check, nobody watches it with monitoring, it is not a DeepCore launch, the Holder Map does not cover its chain) the page shows the part as not available, says why, and leaves its weight out. It is never scored as zero. With less than of the 100 weight points available there is no score at all, only the parts.

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: The score is worked out from a chain and an address and nothing else. No plan, payment, account or workspace is read, so no plan can move it. A Gully Security review counts only once its report is published, and the page links to it with its finding counts. A draft or private report counts for nothing. There is no badge to buy. Watching a contract with monitoring, on any plan, adds the “recent privileged changes” part for everyone, good or bad. Choosing whether a watched contract is listed on /score does not change its score.

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: In the app’s Security tab, a workspace adds a contract (chain and address). It is read every minute through our RPC failover: owner, admin and role changes, upgrades (ERC-1967 and beacon proxies, and a change of the code address found by reading it directly), pauses, signer and threshold changes on the Safe that controls it, and large outflows of its own tokens or coin over the share or amount you set. Each alert is one plain line with a link, sent to Telegram and/or your webhook, and never twice: an event is marked as sent on disk before it goes out, so a restart resumes where it stopped without repeating anything. How many contracts a workspace can watch is part of its plan (pricing). The load is small: about three RPC calls a minute per chain in use, shared by every contract on it, plus about one call a minute per contract.

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: Every score page has a badge (an SVG with the score and the date it was read, in the Gully Labs kit) and a live widget. Both link back to the score page, where every part and its evidence is shown.

chunks.title: Gully Score
chunks.text: Public, read-only and open to any origin. A contract that has not been scored before is worked out on the first request (a few seconds), within a per-address rate limit.

Quoted per project: ask through the form on gullylabs.xyz/security. The aim, as the practice grows, is two reviewers per review, every fix reviewed, and a report published with the client’s consent, pinned to the exact commit hash that was reviewed. Smart-contract audits and code audits Smart-contract audit: a security review plus formal checks of the core maths and accounting, a full fix review and a public report. We will use the word audit for our own work only once there is a public record of reviews and contest results to point to.

Code audit for the non-contract parts: dApp frontends, backends and APIs, key and secret management, wallet-connect and signing flows, infrastructure and CI, checked against a checklist based on the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS).
